verse.text: James, a slave of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes in the Diaspora: greetings.
verse.note: The Greek name is Iakobos, the Greek form of the Hebrew name Jacob. 'James' is how English has come to spell it for New Testament figures. A first-century reader would have heard a man named Jacob addressing 'the twelve tribes', the descendants of the patriarch Jacob.

The Greek word ordinarily means a slave, someone owned by a master, and not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to 'servant' or 'bondservant'. In the Greek Old Testament 'slave of the Lord' is also a title of honour for figures such as Moses, David and the prophets, so the word conveys both total belonging and dignity.

The term was the standard Jewish word for Jews living scattered outside the land of Israel. Whether the letter addresses Jewish followers of Jesus literally living abroad, or uses the phrase as a picture of the whole church as God's scattered people, is disputed.

verse.text: Consider it nothing but joy, my brothers and sisters, whenever you fall into trials of many kinds,
verse.note: The Greek plural, literally 'brothers', was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as fellow members of a family or community. Many recent translations render it 'brothers and sisters' for that reason; older ones have 'brethren' or 'brothers'.

The same Greek word-family covers both an external trial that tests a person and an inner temptation to do wrong. It is rendered 'trial' in verses 2 and 12, where hardship to be endured is in view, and 'tempt' in verses 13–14, where enticement to evil is in view. English cannot keep the single word that links these passages in the Greek, and some interpreters read 'testing' throughout.

verse.text: knowing that the testing of your faith produces endurance.
And let endurance have its perfect work, so that you may be perfect and whole, lacking in nothing.
verse.note: The Greek word means complete, having reached its goal, fully grown; it does not by itself mean flawless or sinless. Many modern versions have 'mature' for persons here. 'Perfect' is kept so that the repetition in this verse and the links to the 'perfect gift' (verse 17) and 'perfect law' (verse 25) stay visible.

verse.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives to all without reservation and without reproach, and it will be given to him.
verse.note: The adverb basically means 'simply, with singleness of purpose', and so 'without holding back'. Most translations have 'generously', which is a possible extension of that sense. The rendering here keeps the contrast with the 'double-minded' person of verse 8: God gives with an undivided mind.

verse.text: But let him ask in faith, doubting nothing, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea, driven and tossed by the wind.
For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord,
a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.
Let the lowly brother boast in his high standing,
and the rich one in his being brought low, because like a flower of the grass he will pass away.
verse.note: The Greek does not repeat 'brother', so it is unclear whether the rich person is a fellow believer told to take pride in being humbled, or an outsider whose only 'boast' is, ironically, his coming downfall. Both readings have scholarly support. The translation leaves the question as open as the Greek does.

verse.text: For the sun rises with its scorching heat and dries up the grass, and its flower falls, and the beauty of its appearance is lost. So too the rich one will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.
Blessed is the man who endures trial, because once he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have no expressed subject: 'which he has promised'. Later manuscripts supply 'the Lord' or 'God'. 'God' is supplied here only because English 'he' would wrongly seem to refer to the person who endures.

verse.text: No one who is being tempted should say, “I am being tempted by God.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one.
But each person is tempted by his own desire, dragged away and lured by it.
Then desire, once it has conceived, bears sin, and sin, once it is full-grown, gives birth to death.
Do not be deceived, my beloved brothers and sisters.
All good giving and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow cast by turning.
Of his own will he gave birth to us by the word of truth, so that we would be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for a mother giving birth. It is the same verb used in verse 15 of sin giving birth to death, and the contrast is deliberate. Older versions used the father's verb 'begat' or the neutral 'brought forth'; several modern versions have 'gave us birth'.

verse.text: Know this, my beloved brothers and sisters. Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger,
verse.note: The Greek form can be either a command ('Know this') or a statement ('You know this'). Some later manuscripts read 'Therefore' instead, which lies behind the King James Version's 'Wherefore'. It is also unclear whether the phrase points back to verses 17–18 or forward to what follows.

verse.text: for a man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness of God.
Therefore, putting away all filthiness and the overflow of wickedness, receive with gentleness the implanted word, which is able to save your souls.
verse.note: The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a humble, unassertive disposition, here the opposite of the anger of verses 19–20. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: But be doers of the word and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.
For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks in a mirror at the face he was born with;
for he looks at himself and goes away, and at once forgets what he was like.
But the one who peers into the perfect law, the law of freedom, and stays with it, becoming not a hearer who forgets but a doer who acts, that one will be blessed in his doing.
If anyone thinks he is religious while not bridling his tongue but deceiving his own heart, that person’s religion is worthless.
verse.note: The Greek word refers to the outward practice of worship (rites, observances and acts of devotion), not to a system of beliefs, which is what 'religion' often means today. The point is that the true observance God accepts is control of the tongue, care for the vulnerable and a clean life.

verse.text: Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to look after orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself unstained by the world.
My brothers and sisters, surely you do not hold faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ while practicing favoritism?

note.traditional: do not hold the faith … with partiality (a command)

verse.note: Most English versions read this sentence as a command. The Greek edition translated here punctuates it as a question, and the negative used expects the answer no. The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so either reading is possible, and the point is the same either way: faith and favoritism do not belong together.

note.term: faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ
note.traditional: the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of the glory.' Most interpreters take it as faith in Jesus, though it can also be read as the faithfulness of Jesus. The closing words 'of the glory' are awkward: they may describe the Lord as glorious, as here, or stand as a title, 'Jesus Christ, the Glory.'

verse.text: For if a man wearing gold rings and splendid clothing comes into your assembly, and a poor person in filthy clothing also comes in,
verse.note: The Greek word is synagoge, the ordinary term for a gathering and for a Jewish synagogue. James uses it for a meeting of Jesus-followers, one sign of how Jewish the setting of this letter is. In 5:14 he uses the word usually translated 'church.'

verse.text: and you look attentively at the one wearing the splendid clothing and say, “You sit here in a good place,” and to the poor person you say, “You stand, or sit there down by my footstool,”
have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?
verse.note: The verb can also mean to be divided or to waver, the sense it has in 1:6, which would give 'are you not divided within yourselves?' On that reading the fault is an inner inconsistency between faith and behavior. Most translations take it as discrimination between people, as here.

verse.text: Listen, my beloved brothers and sisters. Did God not choose those who are poor in the eyes of the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom he promised to those who love him?
But you have dishonored the poor person. Is it not the rich who oppress you, and is it not they who drag you into court?
Is it not they who blaspheme the good name that was invoked over you?
verse.note: To have a name called over someone is a Septuagint idiom for belonging to the one named, used of Israel as God's people. Here the name is most likely that of Jesus. Many see a reference to its being spoken at baptism, though the text does not say so.

verse.text: If, however, you are carrying out the royal law in accordance with the scripture, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” you do well.
verse.note: 'Royal' may mean the law that belongs to the king, or to the kingdom mentioned in verse 5. It may instead mean the law that rules over the other commands. The quotation is from Leviticus 19:18.

verse.text: But if you show favoritism, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.
For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of it all.
For the one who said, “Do not commit adultery,” also said, “Do not murder.” Now if you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.
So speak and so act as people who are going to be judged by a law of freedom.
For judgment is merciless to the one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.
What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone claims to have faith but has no works? Can that faith save them?
If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking daily food,
verse.note: The Greek word often means 'naked' but was also used of someone wearing only an undergarment or lacking adequate clothing, which is the likely sense here. Several modern versions translate similarly.

verse.text: and one of you says to them, “Go in peace; keep warm and eat your fill,” but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it?
So too faith by itself, if it has no works, is dead.
But someone will say, “You have faith, and I have works.” Show me your faith apart from the works, and I will show you my faith by my works.

note.term: You have faith, and I have works.
note.traditional: Thou hast faith, and I have works: shew me thy faith without thy works… (quotation extended)

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks, and where the objector's words end is one of the most debated questions in the letter. The text follows the most common view: the objection is this one sentence, meaning roughly 'one person has faith, another has works,' and James replies from 'Show me.' Others extend the quotation to the end of the verse or beyond, which makes the speaker an ally of James and not an opponent.

verse.text: You believe that God is one? You do well. Even the demons believe, and they shudder.

note.traditional: there is one God / God is one

verse.note: This echoes the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), the central Jewish confession. 'Believe' is the verb form of the word translated 'faith' throughout the chapter, so the point is that faith of this bare kind is something even demons have. Some manuscripts read 'there is one God.'

verse.text: But do you want to know, you empty person, that faith apart from works does not work?

note.traditional: is useless / is barren (KJV: is dead)

verse.note: The Greek adjective means idle or unproductive, literally 'not working,' and James is punning on 'works.' The rendering keeps the pun, where most versions have 'useless' or 'barren.' Many later manuscripts read 'dead' here, as in verses 17 and 26, and that reading lies behind the King James Version.

verse.text: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar?
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: 'justified' is the verb that goes with 'righteousness' in verse 23. It can mean to declare someone in the right or to show them to be in the right, and some translators prefer 'vindicated' or 'shown to be righteous' in James. Paul uses the same verb and the same Genesis text to say a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law (Romans 3:28; 4:2–3). Most interpreters hold that the two writers use 'faith' and 'works' differently and are answering different questions, though how far they agree is debated.

verse.text: You see that faith was working together with his works, and by the works his faith was made complete,
and the scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.
verse.note: The quotation is Genesis 15:6. Abraham is called God's friend in Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7, and the title was common in Jewish writing of the period.

verse.text: You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.
In the same way, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by a different road?
For just as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so too faith apart from works is dead.
Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers and sisters, since you know that we will receive a stricter judgment.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, not males only. James is writing to whole congregations, so 'brothers and sisters' gives what the first readers would have heard. Many recent translations do the same; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

verse.text: For we all stumble in many ways. If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is a perfect man, able to bridle the whole body as well.
Now if we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we guide their whole body as well.
verse.note: Some manuscripts read 'Look' (ide) instead of 'Now if' (ei de); the two were pronounced almost identically in this period. The older English tradition followed the first reading. Most modern editions prefer 'Now if', and the sense is little affected.

verse.text: Look at ships too: though they are so large and are driven by harsh winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the helmsman's impulse directs.
So too the tongue is a small part of the body, and it boasts of great things. See how small a fire kindles how great a forest!

And the tongue is a fire. The tongue is set among the parts of our body as the world of unrighteousness; it stains the whole body, sets ablaze the wheel of existence, and is itself set ablaze by Gehenna.
verse.note: The grammar and punctuation of this verse are notoriously difficult. The phrase may describe the tongue (it stands among the body's parts as the unrighteous world in miniature), or it may be attached to 'fire' in the previous clause. A minority take the word in its other sense, 'adornment', meaning that the tongue makes wrongdoing attractive. The rendering here follows the most common reading.

note.traditional: the course of nature / the whole course of life

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'the wheel of birth' or 'of becoming'. Similar phrases appear in Greek religious and philosophical writing for the cycle of life, and by this period the image seems to have been a general expression for the whole round of human existence. Most translations paraphrase as 'the course of life'. Keeping 'wheel' preserves the image, though exactly what James had in mind is uncertain.

Gehenna is a place name, the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, which had become the Jewish term for the place of final fiery judgment. 'Hell' merges it with Hades and with later imagery, so the name is kept. Many translations still use 'hell', usually with a footnote giving Gehenna.

verse.text: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, is being tamed and has been tamed by humankind,
but the tongue no human being can tame: a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
With it we bless the Lord and Father, and with it we curse people, who have been made in the likeness of God.
verse.note: The phrase echoes the Greek version of Genesis 1:26, where humanity is made 'according to our image and likeness'. The point is that cursing a person insults the God whose likeness that person bears.

verse.text: Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers and sisters, these things ought not to be so.
Does a spring gush sweet and bitter water from the same opening?
Can a fig tree, my brothers and sisters, produce olives, or a grapevine figs? Neither can salt water produce sweet.
Who among you is wise and understanding? Let him show his works by his good way of life, in the gentleness of wisdom.
verse.note: 'Meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a humble, unassertive manner, here set against the jealousy and ambition of the next verse. 'Gentleness' or 'humility' is the mainstream modern rendering.

verse.text: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth.
verse.note: This word is rare outside the New Testament. Its earlier attested use is for self-seeking pursuit of position, which supports 'selfish ambition', the choice of most modern translations. Older versions connected it with a similar-looking word for strife and rendered it 'strife' or 'contention'. Some scholars prefer 'rivalry' or 'party spirit'.

verse.text: This wisdom is not the kind that comes down from above; it is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.
verse.note: The adjective comes from the word for 'soul' or 'life' and describes what belongs to ordinary human life as opposed to what comes from God's Spirit. 'Natural' is the more literal alternative, but in modern English that sounds like praise. The older 'sensual' wrongly suggests bodily appetite.

verse.text: For where there is jealousy and selfish ambition, there is disorder and every base deed.
But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peaceable, forbearing, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without pretense.
verse.note: The word describes someone reasonable and fair, who does not insist on the full letter of their rights. It is usually translated 'gentle'. Here it is kept distinct from the different Greek word rendered 'gentleness' in verse 13. 'Considerate' and 'reasonable' are other common renderings.

The word can mean 'making no distinctions', which gives 'impartial', or 'undivided, unwavering'. The related verb is used in both ways in this letter, for doubting in 1:6 and for discriminating between people in 2:4. Translators and commentators are divided; the second option would give 'unwavering'.

verse.text: And the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verse.note: The Greek can equally mean 'for those who make peace', so that the peacemakers are the ones who benefit from the harvest and not those who sow it. 'The fruit of righteousness' may also mean either the fruit that consists of righteousness or the fruit that righteousness produces. Most translations choose 'by', as here.

verse.text: Where do wars come from, and where do fights among you come from? Is it not from this: your pleasures, which are on campaign in the parts of your body?
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for pleasure or enjoyment (the root of 'hedonism'), not a word for desire. Most English versions render it 'passions' or 'desires' because James pictures the pleasures as a driving force. 'Pleasures' is kept here and in verse 3 so the reader sees the same word both times: the pursuit of enjoyment is what is at war within them.

verse.text: You desire and do not have; you murder and covet and cannot obtain; you fight and wage war. You do not have because you do not ask.

note.term: you murder and covet and cannot obtain

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and the sentence can be divided differently: 'You desire and do not have, so you murder; you covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and wage war.' The translation follows the punctuation of the SBLGNT. 'Murder' is startling in a letter to congregations, and some scholars take it as hyperbole or as the end point of unchecked desire. A long-standing conjecture reads 'you envy' instead, but no manuscript supports it.

verse.text: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your pleasures.
Adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? So whoever chooses to be a friend of the world is made an enemy of God.

note.traditional: You adulterous people / Ye adulterers and adulteresses

verse.note: The Greek is a feminine plural, literally 'adulteresses'. James is drawing on the prophets' picture of God's people as an unfaithful wife (as in Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel); he is not singling out women or speaking of sexual sin. Most modern versions paraphrase as 'adulterous people'. Later manuscripts added 'adulterers and', which is the source of the King James wording.

verse.text: Or do you think the scripture speaks to no purpose when it says, “The spirit he made to dwell in us yearns enviously”?

note.term: “The spirit he made to dwell in us yearns enviously”?
note.traditional: He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us

verse.note: This is one of the most disputed sentences in the letter. 'The spirit' can be either subject or object. Many modern versions take God as the subject, jealously longing for the spirit he placed in us, which suits the image of the unfaithful wife in verse 4. The reading chosen here takes the human spirit as the subject, because the word for envy (phthonos) is always a vice in Greek usage and is not otherwise used of God's jealousy. On this reading verse 6 answers the problem: God gives a grace greater than that envy.

No passage in the Hebrew Bible or its Greek translation matches these words. James may be summarizing the general teaching of Scripture, citing a writing now lost, or, as some propose, the question about Scripture may end before the quoted words and point ahead to the proverb in verse 6. The matter is unresolved.

verse.text: But he gives greater grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the arrogant, but to the humble he gives grace.”
verse.note: The quotation is Proverbs 3:34 in its Greek form. The traditional 'the proud' is accurate, but in modern English 'proud' is often a compliment. The Greek word is always negative and describes people who hold themselves above others, so 'arrogant' is used.

verse.text: So submit to God. But resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.
Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will lift you up.

Do not speak against one another, brothers and sisters. Whoever speaks against a brother or sister, or judges them, speaks against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge.
There is one lawgiver and judge, the one who is able to save and to destroy. But you, who are you to judge your neighbor?
Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will travel to such-and-such a city and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”—
you who do not know what tomorrow holds or what your life will be! For you are a mist that appears for a little while and then disappears.

note.term: what tomorrow holds or what your life will be

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and the manuscripts differ in small ways here. It can also be read as a single clause, 'you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow', or with a separate question, 'What is your life?', as in many versions. The sense is the same on all three readings: the planners cannot see even one day ahead.

verse.text: Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will both live and do this or that.”
But as it is, you boast in your pretensions. All such boasting is evil.
verse.note: The word describes the manner of the braggart who claims more than he has or can deliver. Here it is the confident assumption that one controls the future. Most versions use 'arrogance'. 'Pretensions' keeps the idea of empty claims and stays distinct from the different Greek word translated 'arrogant' in verse 6.

verse.text: So whoever knows the good they ought to do and does not do it, for that person it is sin.
Come now, you rich people, weep and howl over the miseries that are coming upon you.
Your wealth has rotted, and your clothes have become moth-eaten.
Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have stored up treasure in the last days.

note.traditional: will eat your flesh like fire

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and 'like fire' can go with either sentence. Most translations attach it to what precedes, as here. The Greek edition translated here places the break earlier, which would give 'It is fire, as it were, that you have stored up in the last days.' Either division is possible.

verse.text: Look, the wages of the workers who mowed your fields, the wages you kept back, are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

note.traditional: Lord of Sabaoth; Lord of hosts; Lord Almighty

verse.note: James keeps the Hebrew word Sabaoth, 'armies', as the Greek version of Isaiah often does. The title presents God as commander of the heavenly armies, and it is used here for the one who hears the cries of defrauded workers. 'Hosts' is the long-established English form of the title.

verse.text: You have lived on the earth in luxury and self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.
You have condemned, you have murdered the righteous one. Does he not oppose you?

note.traditional: the just; the righteous person; the innocent one

verse.note: One Greek word covers what English divides into 'righteous', 'just' and 'innocent'. Most interpreters take it generically here, of the innocent poor whom the rich ruin through the courts. A minority see a reference to Jesus, who is called 'the Righteous One' elsewhere in the New Testament.

Most translations read this as a statement, 'he does not resist you', picturing a victim who cannot fight back. The Greek edition translated here punctuates it as a question. On that reading the one who now opposes the rich is either the righteous victim or God, of whom the same verb is used in 4:6. Both readings are grammatical, and the choice rests on punctuation that the earliest manuscripts did not have.

verse.text: Be patient, therefore, brothers and sisters, until the coming of the Lord. Look, the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient over it until it receives the early and the late rain.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and James is writing to whole communities. Older translations have 'brethren' or 'brothers', while many recent ones have 'brothers and sisters'. The longer phrase is used here because 'brothers' alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed.

note.term: the early and the late rain
note.traditional: the early and the late rains

verse.note: The Greek has only 'early and late'; 'rain' is understood, and some manuscripts add it. In the eastern Mediterranean the autumn rains soften the ground for sowing and the spring rains swell the grain before harvest. A farmer depends on both, and the pairing is a stock phrase from Israel's Scriptures.

verse.text: You too must be patient. Strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord has drawn near.
Do not grumble against one another, brothers and sisters, so that you may not be judged. Look, the judge is standing at the doors.
Brothers and sisters, take as an example of suffering hardship and of patience the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.
Look, we call blessed those who endured. You have heard of the endurance of Job, and you have seen the outcome the Lord brought about, that the Lord is deeply compassionate and merciful.
verse.note: 'The patience of Job' is proverbial in English, but the Greek word here is not the one translated 'patience' in verses 7–10. It means holding out under pressure, which suits a Job who protests loudly yet does not give up on God. Most modern translations likewise use 'endurance', 'perseverance' or 'steadfastness'.

note.term: the outcome the Lord brought about
note.traditional: the end of the Lord; the purpose of the Lord

verse.note: Literally 'the end of the Lord'. The word can mean an outcome or a goal, so the phrase is either what the Lord finally did for Job, the restoration at the close of the book, or the Lord's purpose in the whole affair. Most interpreters prefer the first sense, which is followed here.

verse.text: Above all, my brothers and sisters, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or with any other oath. Let your yes be yes and your no be no, so that you do not fall under judgment.
Is anyone among you suffering hardship? Let them pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let them sing praise.
Is anyone among you sick? Let them call for the elders of the assembly, and let the elders pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, and in the Greek Scriptures Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and its reference is clear, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader sees one word for one Greek word.

verse.text: And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise them up; and if they have committed sins, they will be forgiven.

note.traditional: will save the sick; will make the sick person well

verse.note: The Greek verb means to rescue, and is used both of healing from illness and of final salvation. Here physical recovery is in view first, and many translations render it 'make well' or 'restore'. 'Save' is kept because the next clauses speak of forgiveness and because the same verb returns in verse 20. 'Raise up' can likewise mean getting up from a sickbed or resurrection.

verse.text: So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be healed. The petition of a righteous person has great power as it takes effect.

note.traditional: the effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much

verse.note: The Greek participle can be read as 'when it is at work', that is, in its effect, or as 'when it is made effective', that is, by God. Older translations took it as describing the prayer's intensity ('fervent'). The meaning is disputed, and the rendering here follows the first reading.

verse.text: Elijah was a human being with a nature like ours, and he prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three years and six months.
verse.note: The story is in 1 Kings 17–18, which says that rain returned 'in the third year' and does not record Elijah praying for the drought. The figure of three and a half years also appears in Luke 4:25 and seems to reflect a Jewish tradition of retelling the story.

verse.text: Then he prayed again, and the sky gave rain, and the earth produced its fruit.
My brothers and sisters, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone turns them back,
let that person know that whoever turns a sinner back from their wandering way will save their soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.

note.traditional: shall save a soul from death; will save his soul from death

verse.note: The Greek 'his soul' does not say whose, and the English 'their' leaves it equally open. Most interpreters take it as the sinner's soul, rescued from death, but the sins covered could be the sinner's or the rescuer's. The word translated 'soul' means the person's life or self, not a separable part of them. Manuscripts also vary slightly in the wording of this phrase.
